📜 'Guard Your Foot' — Rabbi Yonatan and Rava read Ecclesiastes 4:17 as a lesson on sin, sacrifice and repentance
🏠 Tefillin and the Bathroom — regular vs. makeshift bathrooms, and Rava's fear that one will forget them on his head
🐭 From Mice to Prostitutes — how the enactment to hold tefillin in one's hand evolved
💧 'What I Permitted Here I Prohibited There' — refuting Rava and finding the answer in ricocheting drops
🛏️ Tefillin at a Meal, With Money, Under the Pillow — Rav Ḥisda, Abaye, Shmuel and a baraita that refutes him

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Bodily Needs, Prayer, and Where Tefillin May Go
overview.subtitle: Berakhot 23a–23b
overview.hebrewSource: הַנִּצְרָךְ לִנְקָבָיו — אַל יִתְפַּלֵּל, וְאִם הִתְפַּלֵּל — תְּפִלָּתוֹ תּוֹעֵבָה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens by finishing a dispute about one who needed to urinate in the middle of the Amida: Rav Ashi explains that everyone agrees a long delay sends him back to the beginning, and the argument is only about whether his prayer was ever valid. From there the Gemara rules that one who needs to relieve himself may not pray at all, unless he can restrain himself for the time it takes to walk a parasang, and derives it from 'Prepare to greet your God, O Israel'. The rest of the daf is a practical guide to tefillin in undignified places: what to do with them at a regular or makeshift bathroom, the tragic incident that led the Sages to require holding them in one's hand, whether the baraita forbidding urination while wearing them follows Beit Shammai, and finally whether tefillin may be brought to a meal, bundled with coins, or placed under one's pillow.

slides.title: 🚻 May One Who Needs to Relieve Himself Pray?
slides.subtitle: The baraita, its qualification, and the verse behind it

nodes.content: ❓ Rav Ḥisda and Rav Hamnuna disputed one who needed to urinate mid-prayer. Rav Ashi: if the issue were the length of the delay, they would have said so!

💡 Rav Ashi: everyone agrees that a delay long enough to finish the whole prayer sends him back to the start. They argue only where he did not delay: is he גַּבְרָא דְחוּיָא (disqualified, prayer invalid) or גַּבְרָא חַזְיָא (fit, prayer valid)?
📜 Baraita: one who needs to relieve himself may not pray, and if he prayed, his prayer is an abomination (תּוֹעֵבָה)

columns.label: Cannot restrain himself
columns.content: The baraita applies: he may not pray (Rav Zevid, some say Rav Yehuda)

columns.label: Can restrain himself
columns.content: His prayer is valid. For how long? Rav Sheshet (or Rav Zevid): the time it takes to walk a parasang (עַד פַּרְסָה)

nodes.content: ✅ Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: the source is הִכּוֹן לִקְרַאת אֱלֹהֶיךָ יִשְׂרָאֵל, 'Prepare to greet your God, O Israel' (Amos 4:12)

callout.label: Rav Ashi's one-liner:
callout.text: Rav Ashi (some say Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappa) reads 'Guard your foot when you go to the house of God' (Ecclesiastes 4:17) as: שְׁמוֹר נְקָבֶיךָ בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁאַתָּה עוֹמֵד בִּתְפִלָּה לְפָנַי — mind your orifices when you stand before Me in prayer.

slides.title: 🏠 Tefillin at the Bathroom: Who Says What
slides.subtitle: Two baraitot, one dilemma, and three tannaitic positions
rows: Remove tefillin four cubits away, then enter
Remove them and relieve himself immediately; on leaving, walk four cubits before donning
By using it he has made the spot a regular bathroom
Entering a regular bathroom with tefillin only to urinate
Ravina permits, Rav Adda bar Mattana forbids; Rava: forbidden
Lest he come to defecate in them — or, some say, break wind in them
Remove at four cubits, place in the window facing the public domain, enter; on exit walk four cubits before donning
Removes them but holds them in his hand and enters
Holds them in his garment — the Gemara corrects: in his garment and in his hand
In the garment alone he might forget them and they would fall

callout.label: Where not to leave them:
callout.text: The baraita adds: place them in holes near the bathroom, not in holes facing the public domain, lest passersby take them and he come under suspicion (וְיָבֹא לִידֵי חֲשָׁד).

slides.title: 🐭 How the Enactment Evolved: Hold Them in Your Hand
slides.subtitle: Two baraitot tell the story, and the Amoraim fix the details

steps.content: 1️⃣ At first they placed tefillin in holes near the bathroom — mice came and took them
2️⃣ They moved them to windows facing the public domain — passersby came and took them
3️⃣ A student left his tefillin in such a hole; a prostitute took them and announced in the study hall, 'See what so-and-so gave me as my payment.' He went up to the roof, fell and died
4️⃣ At that moment they instituted that one holds them in his garment and in his hand and enters
5️⃣ Rabbi Meyasha son of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: roll them up like a scroll and hold them in the right hand opposite the heart; Rav Naḥman: no strap may hang more than a handbreadth below the hand

6️⃣ Rabbi Zeira / Rabbi Yoḥanan: that is by day, when there is still time to don them; at night he makes a pouch of a handbreadth (כְּמִין כִּיס טֶפַח). Abaye: a handbreadth is needed only for their regular vessel — a different vessel may be smaller

callout.label: Proof for Abaye:
callout.text: Mar Zutra (some say Rav Ashi): small sealed vessels of less than a handbreadth protect their contents even in a tent over a corpse — so a small space can serve as a barrier. And Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rav Naḥman would hand their students a book of aggada before entering the bathroom but kept their tefillin: 'since the Sages permitted it, they will protect me.'

slides.title: 💧 Is the Baraita Beit Shammai? 'What I Permitted Here I Prohibited There'
slides.subtitle: A baraita forbids urinating while holding tefillin — Rava says it is not the halakha

lines.speaker: Baraita
lines.text: One may not hold tefillin in his hand or a Torah scroll in his arm and pray; one may not urinate with them or sleep with them, neither a deep sleep nor a nap. Shmuel adds: a knife, money, a bowl or a loaf are the same — worry that they will fall distracts from prayer.

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: In the name of Rav Sheshet: the halakha does not follow this baraita, for it is Beit Shammai. If it were Beit Hillel — they permit holding tefillin in a regular bathroom to defecate; must it be said that one may hold them to urinate in a makeshift one?

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: The same baraita says, 'Matters which I permitted you here, I prohibited you there.' Is that not tefillin? For Beit Hillel it makes sense: permitted in the regular bathroom, prohibited in the makeshift one. But Beit Shammai permit nothing at all!

lines.speaker: Defense
lines.text: Perhaps 'here and there' refers to baring a handbreadth behind and two in front — one baraita for defecation, another for urination?

lines.speaker: Rejection
lines.text: For urination why bare anything behind? Rather both baraitot are about defecation: two handbreadths in front for a man, none for a woman. But then why call it 'a kal vaḥomer with no refutation'? That is simply how things are. So it must be tefillin — and Rava's statement is conclusively refuted (תְּיוּבְתָּא).

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Then how is the makeshift bathroom stricter? In a regular bathroom one sits and there are no ricocheting drops (נִיצוֹצוֹת), so holding tefillin is permitted; in a makeshift one there are drops he may touch, so it is prohibited. Derive it from this reason, not from a kal vaḥomer — because as a kal vaḥomer it could not be refuted.

callout.label: Method:
callout.text: The Gemara ends up accepting the baraita as Beit Hillel: the leniency for the regular bathroom and the stringency for the makeshift one are both about keeping tefillin clean, not about which house of study one follows.

slides.title: 🛏️ Tefillin at Meals, With Money, and Under the Pillow
slides.subtitle: Three more practical questions close the daf

boxes.title: At a formal meal
items: Baraita: before a regular meal, pace four cubits ten times or ten cubits four times, relieve yourself, then enter
Rabbi Yitzḥak: remove tefillin before entering
Rabbi Ḥiyya disagrees: place them on the table — and that is admirable
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: he refrains until the time of the blessing after the meal

boxes.title: Bundled with coins
items: One baraita permits bundling tefillin with money in one's head covering; another forbids
Rav Ḥisda: forbidden only if the cloth was designated for tefillin and already used; designated only, or used only — permitted
Abaye, who holds designation is significant (הַזְמָנָה מִילְּתָא הִיא): designated alone is enough to forbid; used without designation — permitted

boxes.title: Under his head at night
items: Rav Yosef son of Rav Neḥunya asked Rav Yehuda: under the feet is obviously degrading — what about under the head?
Shmuel: permitted, even if his wife is with him
Baraita: under the head is fine, but if his wife is with him it is forbidden — unless the spot is three handbreadths higher or lower
A conclusive refutation of Shmuel — yet Rava rules like Shmuel anyway. Why? The daf ends on the question

callout.label: Note:
callout.text: In two of these three cases the daf sides with dignity plus practicality: tefillin should be protected, but not treated as an ordinary object one bundles with cash or sleeps on.

summary.principle: Prayer requires a body at rest and a clear mind, and tefillin demand dignity even in the bathroom — so the Sages built a chain of enactments to keep them safe, clean and close to their owner.

flowSteps.content: 🚻 Needs to relieve himself → may not pray; his prayer is an abomination — unless he can hold on for a parasang (Amos 4:12: 'Prepare to greet your God')
🏠 Regular bathroom: remove tefillin four cubits away. Makeshift: remove and go at once. Rava: never enter a regular bathroom wearing them, even to urinate

columns.content: 🐭 Holes near the bathroom → mice; windows to the street → passersby and the prostitute incident → hold them in garment and hand, rolled like a scroll
💧 Baraita forbidding urination with tefillin in hand is Beit Hillel after all: regular bathroom has no ricocheting drops, makeshift does

flowSteps.content: 🛏️ Meal: R' Yitzḥak removes, R' Ḥiyya sets them on the table. Money: Rav Ḥisda needs designation + use, Abaye designation alone. Under the head: Shmuel permits even with his wife — refuted, yet Rava rules like him
🎓 Key Principle: Halakha protects both the person praying (no distraction, no discomfort) and the sanctity of tefillin (no filth, no theft, no degradation)

quiz.q: According to Rav Ashi, what do Rav Ḥisda and Rav Hamnuna actually disagree about regarding one who needed to urinate mid-prayer?
o: Whether a delay long enough to finish the whole prayer sends him back to the beginning
Whether, when he did not delay that long, his prayer was valid at all — was he a fit person or a disqualified one?
Whether he may finish praying before relieving himself
Whether the rule applies to Shema as well as the Amida
quiz.e: Rav Ashi notes that the dispute never mentions the length of delay. Everyone agrees a long delay requires starting over; they argue whether, absent such a delay, the person was fit for prayer (prayer valid) or disqualified (prayer invalid).

quiz.q: One who needs to relieve himself but can restrain himself may still pray. For how long must he be able to hold on?
o: Until he finishes the entire Amida
The time it takes to walk a parasang
Until midnight
The time it takes to walk four cubits
quiz.e: Rav Zevid (or Rav Yehuda) limits the baraita to one who cannot restrain himself, and Rav Sheshet (or Rav Zevid) sets the measure at the time it takes to walk a parasang.

quiz.q: Why did Rava forbid entering a regular bathroom wearing tefillin even just to urinate?
o: Because Beit Shammai forbid bringing tefillin near a bathroom at all
Because urine splashes on the tefillin straps
Because we are concerned he will come to defecate, or break wind, while still wearing them
Because the tefillin would become impure in the bathroom
quiz.e: Ravina permitted and Rav Adda bar Mattana forbade; Rava ruled it forbidden lest he defecate in them, and some say lest he forget they are on his head and break wind in them.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara finally explain 'matters which I permitted you here, I prohibited you there' with respect to tefillin?
o: Beit Shammai permit holding tefillin in a makeshift bathroom but not a regular one
In a regular bathroom one sits and there are no ricocheting drops, so holding tefillin is permitted; in a makeshift bathroom there are drops, so it is prohibited
It refers to baring one handbreadth behind and two in front
It refers to a man versus a woman
quiz.e: After the intermediate suggestions about handbreadths are rejected, the Gemara concludes the baraita is about tefillin and Rava's attribution to Beit Shammai is refuted. The distinction is the ricocheting drops in a makeshift bathroom, to be derived by reason rather than by kal vaḥomer.

quiz.q: According to Abaye, who holds that designation is significant, when is it forbidden to bundle money in a cloth used for tefillin?
o: Only if the cloth was designated for tefillin and tefillin were already bundled in it
Only if tefillin were already bundled in it, regardless of designation
If the cloth was designated for tefillin, even if tefillin were never yet bundled in it
Never — money and tefillin may always be bundled together
quiz.e: Rav Ḥisda requires both designation and actual use. Abaye, for whom designation itself is significant, forbids as soon as the cloth was designated, while use without designation does not forbid.
